Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs) have modest sensitivity, but are highly specific in diagnosing GPA when present. C
Treatment is aimed at inducing remission with rituximab or cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids and maintaining remission with rituximab, azathioprine or methotrexate.B

background.definition: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), formerly known as Wegener's granulomatosis, is a multisystem inflammatory disease characterized by granulomatous vasculitis of small arteries and veins in the upper and lower respiratory tracts and the kidneys. It was first described in 1931 by a German medical student; 5 years later, Friedrich Wegener described a similar clinical presentation in 3 patients. It is one of several antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) associated vasculitides. Diagnostic criteria are shown below in the Diagnosis section.

list.listitem: There are between 3 and 20 new cases per million persons per year in the United States.
A systematic review of 32 studies estimated a lower prevalence globally of approximately 1 case per million person-years.
The mean age of onset is 44 years and the peak age of diagnosis occurs between 60 and 70 years.
Men and women are equally affected.
The disease is largely one of whites (95%-97%).
Incidence decreases from north to south in the Northern hemisphere.

The diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis is often delayed because its symptoms are similar to more common problems such as sinusitis. In a British study of 199 patients, the average time to diagnosis after initial presentation was close to 7 months and 92% of patients had a delay of at least 1 month.

A survey of 701 patients in the United States showed earlier diagnoses in the 1990s compared with the 1970s and 1980s, but only 7% of cases were correctly diagnosed on the patient's first visit to a physician.
The cause is unknown.
No definite link to infectious etiologies or to unique genetic markers have been found.
Proteinase-3 (PR3) from neutrophils reacts with circulating ANCAs and adheres to and damage endothelial cells in arterioles and venules located mainly in respiratory and renal tissues.
T cells may be involved; study results are inconclusive to date.
Histopathology reveals a triad of granulomas in the upper or lower respiratory tracts, necrotizing vasculitis of arteries and veins, and segmental glomerulonephritis with or without granulomas.

Suspect granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) in patients with upper respiratory symptoms such as sinusitis, wheezing, purulent or bloody nasal discharge, fever, joint pains, and other symptoms, especially if the patient does not respond to initial treatment. C
Use the 2022 EULAR criteria to make the diagnosis (), with emphasis on ANCA testing and biopsy to support the diagnosis. C
ANCAs have modest sensitivity, but are highly specific in diagnosing GPA.C
When monitored over time, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 97% sensitive in reflecting overall disease severity.C

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: The 2022 EULAR diagnostic criteria are shown in . Patients with 5 or more points have a likely diagnosis of granulomatotis with polyangiitis (GPA).

list.listitem: Suspect granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) in patients with upper respiratory symptoms such as sinusitis, purulent or bloody nasal discharge, fever, or joint pains, especially if the patients do not respond to initial treatment. Patients may also complain of wheezing due to tracheal stenosis.
Approximately two-thirds of patients with GPA have ear, nose, and throat symptoms; 85% have nasal symptoms; and 50% have ear complaints. Facial ulceration is a rare complication.
See for diagnostic criteria.
No one test is definitive. See for diagnostic criteria.

ANCA: In a study of 72 patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), 100 diseased control patients, and 206 healthy blood donors, the sensitivity of anti-PR3 classic enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and capture ELISA in diagnosing GPA were 74% and 87.5%, respectively, with 100% specificity. The indirect immunofluorescence test was 92% sensitive and 100% specific.
In a study of 89 Chinese patients with GPA, 61% had perinuclear ANCA positivity with the myeloperoxidase antigen marker compared with only 38% with PR3 ANCA.
Nonspecific findings include leukocytosis, normochromic normocytic anemia, thrombocytosis, elevated ESR and CRP, and sediment in the urine.
In a retrospective cohort of 33 patients with GPA, 40% of nasal biopsies were abnormal compared with 94% of kidney biopsies.
In 224 patients with GPA from 7 case series, the most common findings on CT or MRI were mucosal thickening (88%), bony destruction (60%) and septal erosion (59%).
Suspect GPA in patients with upper respiratory symptoms such as sinusitis, purulent or bloody nasal discharge, fever, or joint pain, especially if they do not respond to initial treatment.
See for diagnostic criteria, for assessment of severity, and for treatment recommendations from 2021 ACR guidelines.

The Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score, compared with global assessment by physicians, correlates well with disease activity. All 107 patients who were judged to be well had a score of 0. Patients with active disease had median scores of 10. Of the 12 patients who died, the median score was 20.
See for a summary of how to classify disease stage and severity. Treatment regimens according to disease stage are summarized in .C

Treatment of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is aimed at inducing remission with rituximab or cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids and maintaining remission with rituximab, azathioprine or methotrexate.B
Duration of therapy should be guided by the patient's condition, values, and preference and should generally be at least 18 months.C
Follow-up for disease activity and damage at least every 6 months after remission. C
Goals of treatment are to induce remission, improve patient survival, prevent disease relapse and target organ damage, and to minimize therapy-induced toxicity.
Treatment is guided by the extent and severity of disease. See for a summary of how to determine the severity of Wegener's granulomatosis and for a summary of treatment regimens.

Patients with generalized disease or with threatened organ involvement should receive rituximab or cyclophosphamide and steroids. If remission is achieved, switch to maintenance therapy with low dose steroids plus azathioprine after 3 months (oral regimen) and after 3 to 6 months (IV regimen). In both cases, the goal is a maximum of 6 months of therapy.

The ADVOCATE trial randomized 331 patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis to avacopan (a C5a receptor antagonist) 30 mg twice daily or a 20 week tapering dose of prednisone. At 26 weeks there was no difference in remission, which was 72.3% for avacopan versus 70% for prednisone. Sustained remission at one year was more likely with avacopan (65.7% vs 54.9%, p < 0.001, NNT = 9). Serious adverse events were similar between groups.
American College of Rheumatology guidelines from 2021 and EULAR 2022 guidelines are summarized below. Most are based on obsevational studies and lower quality research.

listitem.strong: Induction of remission for severe disease

list.listitem: American College of Rheumatology (ACR) guidelines (2021) for active severe disease recommend rituximab (RTX) over cyclophosphamide. EULAR found similar efficacy cyclophosphamide and RTX with regards to remission induction. However, they concluded that RTX is more effective for patients with relapsing disease.
A systematic review of observational studies reported a complete remission rate of 72% at 6 months and 8% at 12 months.
Patients taking rituximab (RTX) or cyclophosphamide should take low dose TMP-SMX for prophylaxis against pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

IV pulse glucocorticoids or high dose oral glucocorticoids can be added as part of initial therapy in active, severe disease. EULAR guidelines conclude that faster tapering results in similar remission rates but lower rates of serious infections. They also recommend that avacopan can be used to rapidly taper and replace glucocorticoids.

Plasma exchange is not recommended by ACR guidelines in patients with alveolar hemorrhage or active glomerulonephritis. EULAR guidelines note that it may reduce the likelihood of end-stage renal disease at 1 year but not in the long-term.

listitem.strong: Induction of remission for non-severe disease

list.listitem: ACR guidelines (2021) make a conditional recommendation for using methotrexate over cyclophosphamide or rituximab.
Addition of glucocorticoids (GCs) to methotrexate is recommended over other combinations including cyclophosphamide + GCs, mycophenolate mofetil + GCs, and trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole + GCs.

ACR guidelines recommend rituximab over methotrexate or azathiprine for maintenance of remission, although the latter drugs are options. EULAR guidelines also recommend RTX over azathioprine for maintenance of remission.
They recommend against using ANCA iters or CD19+ B cell counts to guide dosage adjustments of rituximab.
Once patients being treated with rituximab have entered remission, use methotrexate or azathiprine over lefulomide or mycophenolate mofetil to maintain remission.

The duration of remission therapy should be guided by the patients clinical condition, values, and preferences. In general, a period of maintenance therapy for at least 18 months should be considered.
During maintenance of remission, the steroid dose should be tapered to prednisolone 10 mg per day, and then further tapered if possible after 6 to 18 months.
Addition of TMP-SMX is not recommended to maintain remission.

Etanercept, an anti-cytokine targeted therapy, does not appear to improve remission or diminish disease flares. Additionally, etanercept and belimumab likely increase withdrawal due to adverse events.
For patients who relapse and are experiencing severe disease while not taking rituximab, rituximab is recommended by EULAR guidelines.
On the other hand, for patients who relapse while taking rituximab, switching to cyclophosphamide is recommended.

An RCT identified 188 patients with relapse of ANCA associated vasculitis, who all reeived rituximab and glucocorticoids for remission. Those achieving remission at 4 months (n=170) were randomized to rituximab IV 1000 mg q 4 months for 20 months) or azathioprine 9mg/kg/day, tapered after 24 months). Patients were then followed for 36 months to monitor for relapse, which was significantly less likely with rituximab (22% vs 36%, HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.27-0.61, NNT = 7).
Consider IV immunoglobulin for patients with disease refractory to medical therapy.
Combined therapy with rituximab plus cyclophosphamide is not recommended.
In patients with refractory disease, other treatment options include mycophenolate mofetil, IV immunoglobulin, anti-thymocyte globulin, alemtuzumab, and stem cell transplant.

There is only a limited number of clinical trials. In a randomized trial of 50 patients with newly diagnosed Wegener's granulomatosis, 67% of patients treated with prednisone plus IV pulse cyclophosphamide achieved remission compared with 56% of patients treated with prednisone plus oral cyclophosphamide. The rate of side effects was the same in each group. However, the mortality rate was 33% and 44%, respectively. In an uncontrolled study, IV methotrexate (0.3 mg/kg once weekly) induced remission in 59% of patients.

In a small randomized trial of patients who achieved remission, those treated with SMX-TMP (800 mg sulfamethoxazole and 160 mg trimethoprim) given twice daily for 24 months were more likely to remain in remission (82%) than those maintained on placebo (60%; NNT = 5). However, a systematic review of 7 studies with 520 patients including 2 RCTs found no evidence that SMX-TMP reduced the relapse rate. One retrospective cohort study found an association of SMX-TMP with a reduced risk of severe infection in patients also taking rituximab. EUVAS guidelines do not recommend it as a sole agent for maintenance of remission.

The use of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) as an adjunct to prednisone and cyclophosphamide in preventing relapse among patients with Wegener's is of uncertain value; IVIG use was associated with disease activity scores but no benefit in mortality, serious adverse events, time-to-relapse, or infection rates.

An RCT identified 188 patients with relapse of ANCA associated vasculitis, who all reeived rituximab and glucocorticoids for remission. Those achieving remission at 4 months (n=170) were randomized to rituximab IV 1000 mg q 4 months for 20 months) or azathioprine 9mg/kg/day, tapered after 24 months). Patients were then followed for 36 months to monitor for relapse, which was significantly less likely with rituximab (22% vs 36%, HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.27-0.61, NNT = 7).

In an uncontrolled study, no patients with subglottic stenosis unresponsive to systemic immunosuppression treated with mechanical dilation of the trachea accompanied by intratracheal injection of glucocorticoid required subsequent tracheostomy.
Plasmapheresis may lead to higher rates of renal recovery and recovery from alveolar hemorrhage.

Approximately 40% of patients will develop chronic renal insufficiency; 35% will develop hearing loss; 28% will develop cosmetic and functional nasal deformities (including saddle-nose); 13% will develop tracheal stenosis; and 8% will develop visual loss.
In patients who have Wegener's granulomatosis for more than 10 years, 15% end up on dialysis and 49% report shortness of breath.
Medication side effects include diabetes, hair loss, cystitis, bladder cancer, myelodysplasia, cataracts, fractures, aseptic necrosis, gonadal dysfunction, and lymphoma.
Since most primary care physicians will not see patients with Wegener's granulomatosis, patients should be referred to a rheumatologist for primary management.
Approximately half of Wegener's patients will have a disease relapse within 2 years. The Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is useful for prognosis.B
With cyclophosphamide treatment, 5-year survival is 82%, but nearly 90% have disease-related morbidity and approximately 40% have morbidity from treatment. B
Monitor CBC, liver function, and renal function before treatment and then frequently thereafter, according to which drugs are used. C
Prior to 1970, 82% of patients with active Wegener's granulomatosis died within 1 year.
Approximately half of Wegener's patients will have a disease relapse within 2 years.
For patients with Wegener's, the standardized mortality ratio is 2.6 (95% CI 2.0-3.4) compared with the general population.

In a series of 22 patients at a university hospital in Turkey, mean survival was 56 months, and prognosis was worse in patients with renal or cardiac involvement. Upper respiratory tract involvement was associated with a better progrnosis and longer survival.
With cyclophosphamide treatment, 5-year survival is 82%, but nearly 90% have disease-related morbidity and approximately 40% have morbidity from treatment.

The Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score (paper version here), compared with global assessment by physicians, correlates well with disease activity. All 107 patients who were judged to be well had a score of 0. Patients with active disease had median scores of 10. Of the 12 patients who died, the median score was 20.

There is controversy over which markers to follow to assess disease activity. Some find the ESR more predictive; others advocate c-ANCA with the PR3 antibody marker. A positive PR3 ANCA is associated with an increased risk of relapse.
Monitor CBC, liver function, and renal function pretreatment and then frequently thereafter according to which drugs are used.
Monitor disease activity with the Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score, and monitor damage with the Vasculitis Damage Index every 6 months.
Elderly patients are more likely to die from this disease.

Of 36 pregnant women with Wegener's granulomatosis, 21 were in remission at the beginning of pregnancy, 11 were given the diagnosis during pregnancy, and 4 had active disease at the beginning of pregnancy. Disease exacerbations occurred in 11 women, mostly in the first and second trimesters.
In these 36 pregnancies, 16 women delivered at term, 13 had cesarean deliveries, 2 had spontaneous abortions, 5 had therapeutic abortions, and 2 women died.

A systematic review identified 6 studies with 92 pregnancies in patients with ANCA associated vasculitis. THey found an 18% prevalence of preterm delivery, 20% of intrauterine growth retardation and 28% of disease flares.

feature.caption: Disease Severity of Wegener's Granulomatosis based on 2021 ACR Guidelines.

tr.td: Active severe disease

New, persistent, or worsening signs and symptoms that are not related to prior damage. Severe disease characterized by life or organ threatening vasculitis including alveolar hemorrhage, glomerulonephritis, CNS or cardiac involvement, mesenteric ischemia, and ischemia or limbs or digits
Active non-severe disease

New, persistent, or worsening signs and symptoms that are not related to prior damage. Non-severe disease does not have life or organ threatening manifestations but may include rhinosinusitis, asthma, uncomplicated cutaneous disease, and mild inflammatory joint involvement
Remission of disease
Patient has not signs or symptoms of disease
Relapse
Active disease that recurs after a period remission, usually several months
Refractory
Disease that persists despite immunosuppressive treatment.
Active severe disease
Rituximab combined with reduced dose glucocorticoids
Cyclophosphamide with reduced dose glucocorticoids
Active non-severe disease
Methotrexate (MTX) + glucocorticoid (GC)
Rituximab + GC, cyclophosphamide + GC, azathioprine + GC
Maintenance of remission following active severe disease
Rituximab
Methotrexate or azathioprine
Maintenance of remission following active non-severe disease
If treated with MTX or azathioprine, continue same medication. If treated with rituximab or cyclophosphamide, consider rituximab, MTX, azathioprine, or leflunomide.
Relapse
If on rituximab switch to cyclophosphamide, if not on rituximab use rituximab
